claim: Fasting results in a significant decrease in mitochondrial size in AgRP neurons compared to feeding (0.130 ± 0.005 µm² vs 0.174 ± 0.007 µm², p<0.0001).
source: compared to feeding (0.174 ± 0.007 µm2, p<0.0001; Figure 1a,c), fasting resulted in a significant decrease in mitochondrial size (0.130 ± 0.005 µm2, Figure 1b,c) in AgRP neurons
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy measurements and statistical analysis showing p<0.0001, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Fasting is associated with a significant increase in mitochondrial density in AgRP neurons (0.551 ± 0.032 mitochondria/µm² of cytosol in fasting vs 0.423 ± 0.026 mitochondria/µm² of cytosol in feeding; p=0.0031).
source: together with a significant increase in mitochondrial density (0.551 ± 0.032 mitochondria/µm2 of cytosol in fasting vs 0.423 ± 0.026 mitochondria/µm2 of cytosol in feeding; p=0.0031; Figure 1d)
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy quantification with statistical significance p=0.0031, referenced in Figure 1d.

claim: Fasting is associated with a decrease in mitochondrial aspect ratio in AgRP neurons (1.629 ± 0.020 in fasting vs 1.769 ± 0.049 in feeding; p=0.0064).
source: This was associated with a decrease in mitochondrial aspect ratio (AR; the ratio between the major and minor axis of the ellipse equivalent to the mitochondrion which is indicative of mitochondrial morphological change; 1.629 ± 0.020 in fasting vs 1.769 ± 0.049 in feeding; p=0.0064; Figure 1e).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy measurements with statistical significance p=0.0064, referenced in Figure 1e.

claim: Total mitochondrial coverage in the cytosol in AgRP neurons was not altered between fed and fasted mice (7.237 ± 0.461% of cytosol vs 6.830 ± 0.363% of cytosol; p=0.4853).
source: However, total mitochondrial coverage in the cytosol (Figure 1f) in AgRP neurons was not altered between fed (7.237 ± 0.461% of cytosol) and fasted mice (6.830 ± 0.363% of cytosol; p=0.4853).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy measurements showing no significant difference (p=0.4853), referenced in Figure 1f.

claim: Food deprivation promotes mitochondrial fission in AgRP neurons.
source: These observations indicate that food deprivation promotes mitochondrial fission in AgRP neurons, consistent with our prior published work (Dietrich et al., 2013).
evidence: Inferred from the observed changes in mitochondrial size, density, and aspect ratio, and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Fasting resulted in a significant increase in Agrp mRNA transcript in the input RNAs compared to fed state (5.248 ± 1.176 vs 1.036 ± 0.132, p=0.00741).
source: We observed that compared to fed state (1.036 ± 0.132, n = 5), fasting resulted in a significant increase in Agrp mRNA transcript in the input RNAs (5.248 ± 1.176, n = 5; p=0.00741, Figure 1g).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data with statistical significance p=0.00741, referenced in Figure 1g.

claim: Agrp mRNA transcripts were enriched by 27-fold in the immunoprecipitated RNAs in fasted AgrpCre:ERT2; RiboTag mice (input = 5.248 ± 1.176 vs IP = 143.998 ± 22.651; p=0.0003).
source: Compared to the input RNAs, Agrp and Npy mRNA transcripts were enriched by 27- and 56-fold in the immunoprecipitated RNAs (IP), respectively, in fasted AgrpCre:ERT2; RiboTag mice (Agrp = input = 5.248 ± 1.176, n = 5; IP = 143.998 ± 22.651, n = 5; p=0.0003, Figure 1g
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from ribosomal tagging with statistical significance p=0.0003, referenced in Figure 1g.

claim: Npy mRNA transcripts were enriched by 56-fold in the immunoprecipitated RNAs in fasted AgrpCre:ERT2; RiboTag mice (input = 2.680 ± 0.996 vs IP = 151.286 ± 51.683; p=0.0207).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from ribosomal tagging with statistical significance p=0.0207, referenced in Figure 1h.

claim: A significant decrease of Pomc mRNA transcript in the IP RNAs was found in fed AgrpCre:ERT2; RiboTag mice (0.203 ± 0.093 vs input 1.062 ± 0.184; p=0.0031).
source: Conversely, a significant decrease of Pomc mRNA transcript in the IP RNAs was found in fed AgrpCre:ERT2; RiboTag mice (0.203 ± 0.093, n = 5; p=0.0031, Figure 1i) compared to the input RNAs (1.062 ± 0.184, n = 5).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from ribosomal tagging with statistical significance p=0.0031, referenced in Figure 1i.

claim: Dnm1l mRNA transcript was significantly upregulated in AgRP neurons of fasted mice compared to fed mice (fasted = 2.095 ± 0.335 vs fed = 0.873 ± 0.337; p=0.0329).
source: In support of our mitochondrial morphology data, quantitative real time-PCR (qRT-PCR) analyses revealed that Dnm1l mRNA transcript (fed = 0.873 ± 0.337, n = 5; fasted = 2.095 ± 0.335, n = 5; p=0.0329, Figure 1k) was significantly upregulated in AgRP neurons of fasted mice compared to fed mice.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data with statistical significance p=0.0329, referenced in Figure 1k.

claim: The percent of AgRP neurons expressing pDRP1 was significantly increased in fasting (49.2 ± 7.228%) compared to the fed condition (22.33 ± 3.921%; p=0.0085).
source: We found that percent of AgRP neurons expressing pDRP1 was significantly increased in fasting (49.2 ± 7.228% of AgRP neurons, n = 6; Figure 1m,o,q,r) compared to the fed condition (22.33 ± 3.921% of AgRP neurons, n = 6, p=0.0085, Figure 1l,n,p,r).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry quantification with statistical significance p=0.0085, referenced in Figure 1.

claim: No changes in AgRP cell number were observed between fed and fasted mice (fed = 152.2 ± 11.14 vs fasted = 160.8 ± 4.028; p=0.4527).
source: No changes in AgRP cell number were observed between fed (152.2 ± 11.14; n = 5; Figure 1s) and fasted mice (160.8 ± 4.028, n = 6; p=0.4527, Figure 1s).
evidence: Supported by cell counting data showing no significant difference (p=0.4527), referenced in Figure 1s.

claim: Activation of AgRP neurons in fasting state is closely associated with increased DRP1 activation and mitochondrial fission.
source: These data suggest that activation of AgRP neurons in fasting state is closely associated with increased DRP1 activation and, thus, mitochondrial fission, suggesting that DRP1-mediated mitochondrial dynamics may play a role in the regulation of AgRP neuronal activity in fasting state.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of increased pDRP1 expression, Dnm1l mRNA upregulation, and mitochondrial fission during fasting.

claim: The hypothalamus is a key region in the control of energy metabolism via the ability of hypothalamic neurons to respond to numerous metabolic signals, including nutrients.
source: The hypothalamus is a key region in the control of energy metabolism via the ability of hypothalamic neurons to respond to numerous metabolic signals, including nutrients (Jin and Diano, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jin and Diano, 2018.

claim: It has been proposed that hypothalamic availability of free fatty acids controls food intake.
source: It has been proposed that hypothalamic availability of free fatty acids controls food intake (Lam et al., 2005) and AgRP function (Andrews et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lam et al., 2005 and Andrews et al., 2008.

claim: About 15% of cells in primary hypothalamic neuronal cultures from Dnm1l+/+-AgrpCre:ERT2; tdTomato mice expressed tdTomato (14.75 ± 1.704%).
source: First, we analyzed the percentage of tdTomato-expressing AgRP neurons in the cultures and found that about 15% of cells expressed tdTomato (14.75 ± 1.704%; Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: Supported by cell counting in culture, referenced in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment of 2 μM 4-hydroxytamoxifen showed no significant difference in the percentage of cell viability compared to vehicle-treated primary hypothalamic neuronal cultures.
source: Treatment of 2 μM 4-hydroxytamoxifen showed no significant difference in the percentage of cell viability compared to vehicle-treated primary hypothalamic neuronal cultures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Supported by trypan blue viability assay, referenced in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e.

claim: In high glucose concentration, the rate of PA-induced oxygen consumption was significantly lower compared to that measured in low glucose.
source: A significant difference in PA-induced mitochondrial maximal oxygen consumption rate was observed in primary hypothalamic neurons according to the amount of glucose present in the culture (Figure 2). In high glucose concentration, the rate of PA-induced oxygen consumption was significantly lower (Figure 2a,b) compared to that measured in low glucose (Figure 2c,d).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse XF96 Analyzer measurements, referenced in Figure 2.

claim: Under both high and low glucose conditions, a significant decrease in maximal oxygen consumption rate was observed by the addition of etomoxir.
source: Furthermore, under both high and low glucose conditions, a significant decrease in maximal oxygen consumption rate was observed by the addition of the etomoxir, inhibitor of carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1 (CPT1), transporter of fatty acids into the mitochondria.
evidence: Supported by Seahorse XF96 Analyzer measurements with etomoxir treatment.

claim: When glucose levels are low, hypothalamic neurons utilize fatty acids, such as palmitate, as substrates for mitochondrial respiration.
source: Together, these data suggest that similar to fasting state, when glucose levels are low, hypothalamic neurons utilize fatty acids, such as palmitate, as substrates for mitochondrial respiration.
evidence: Inferred from the observed increase in palmitate-induced oxygen consumption under low glucose conditions.

claim: Fasted Drp1 cKO mice showed limited pDRP1 expression in AgRP neurons (14.15 ± 0.926%) compared to fasted controls (52.39 ± 3.71%; p<0.0001).
source: To validate our animal model, we analyzed and found limited pDRP1 expression in the AgRP neurons of fasted Drp1 cKO mice (14.15 ± 0.926% of AgRP neurons, n = 4; Figure 3—figure supplement 1b–h) compared to fasted Dnm1l+/+; AgrpCre:ERT2; tdTomato mice (used as control to visualize AgRP neurons; 52.39 ± 3.71% of AgRP neurons, n = 4, p<0.0001, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b–h) by immunohistochemistry analysis.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry quantification with statistical significance p<0.0001, referenced in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No difference in AgRP cell numbers was found between control and Drp1 cKO mice (control = 150.3 ± 4.423 vs Drp1 cKO = 146 ± 3.082; p=0.4605).
source: No difference in AgRP cell numbers was found between control (150.3 ± 4.423 neurons, n = 4) and Drp1 cKO mice (146 ± 3.082 neurons, n = 4, p=0.4605, Figure 3—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: Supported by cell counting showing no significant difference (p=0.4605), referenced in Figure 3—figure supplement 1i.

claim: No differences in mitochondrial size, density, aspect ratio, and coverage were observed between fed and fasted Drp1 cKO male mice.
source: Next, we analyzed mitochondrial morphological changes in AgRP neurons of Drp1 cKO male mice in fed and fasted states. No differences in mitochondrial size (Figure 3a–c), density (Figure 3d), aspect ratio (Figure 3e), and coverage (Figure 3f) were observed between fed and fasted Drp1 cKO male mice, indicating that selective deletion of Dnm1l in AgRP neurons prevents fasted-induced mitochondrial fission.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy measurements, referenced in Figure 3.

claim: Selective deletion of Dnm1l in AgRP neurons prevents fasted-induced mitochondrial fission.
source: No differences in mitochondrial size (Figure 3a–c), density (Figure 3d), aspect ratio (Figure 3e), and coverage (Figure 3f) were observed between fed and fasted Drp1 cKO male mice, indicating that selective deletion of Dnm1l in AgRP neurons prevents fasted-induced mitochondrial fission.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of mitochondrial morphological changes in Drp1 cKO mice during fasting.

claim: About 15% of cells in primary hypothalamic neuronal cultures from Drp1 cKO mice were tdTomato positive (14.70 ± 2.901%).
source: First, similar to control-derived cultures, about 15% of cells were tdTomato positive (Drp1 cKO, 14.70 ± 2.901%; Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–d).
evidence: Supported by cell counting in culture, referenced in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: No significant difference was observed between the percentage of tdTomato positive cells from Dnm1lfl/fl;AgrpCre:ERT2 mice and from Dnm1l+/+; AgrpCre:ERT2 mice (p=0.9883).
source: No significant difference was observed between the percentage of tdTomato positive cells in this group (from Dnm1lfl/fl;AgrpCre:ERT2 mice) and the percentage of tdTomato positive cells derived from Dnm1l+/+; AgrpCre:ERT2 mice shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d (p=0.9883 by two-tailed Student's t-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison (p=0.9883) between two culture groups.

claim: Primary hypothalamic neuronal cells isolated from Dnm1lfl/fl; AgrpCre:ERT2; tdTomato mice showed no significant difference in the percentage of cell viability when treated either with 2 μM 4-hydroxytamoxifen or vehicle.
source: Similar to primary hypothalamic neuronal cells isolated from Dnm1l+/+; AgrpCre:ERT2; tdTomato mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e), primary hypothalamic neuronal cells isolated from Dnm1lfl/fl; AgrpCre:ERT2; tdTomato mice showed no significant difference in the percentage of cell viability when treated either with 2 μM 4-hydroxytamoxifen or vehicle (Figure 3—figure supplement 2e).
evidence: Supported by trypan blue viability assay, referenced in Figure 3—figure supplement 2e.

claim: A significant reduction of Dnm1l mRNA expression was observed in primary hypothalamic neuronal cell cultures treated with 2 μM 4-hydroxytamoxifen derived from Dnm1lfl/fl; AgrpCre:ERT2; tdTomato mice (0.4512 ± 0.2134) compared to cultures from Dnm1l+/+; AgrpCre:ERT2; tdTomato mice (1.037 ± 0.1825; p=0.0493).
source: Furthermore, a significant reduction of Dnm1l mRNA expression was observed in primary hypothalamic neuronal cell cultures treated with 2 μM 4-hydroxytamoxifen derived from Dnm1lfl/fl; AgrpCre:ERT2; tdTomato mice (0.4512 ± 0.2134, n = 4; Figure 3—figure supplement 2f) compared to primary hypothalamic neuronal cell cultures treated with 2 μM 4-hydroxytamoxifen derived from Dnm1l+/+; AgrpCre:ERT2; tdTomato mice (1.037 ± 0.1825, n = 3, p=0.0493, Figure 3—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data with statistical significance p=0.0493, referenced in Figure 3—figure supplement 2f.

claim: No difference in PA-induced maximal oxygen consumption rate was observed in high (2.5 mM) or low glucose (0.5 mM) in primary hypothalamic neuronal cell cultures from Drp1 cKO mice.
source: We then determined PA-induced mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate in primary hypothalamic neuronal cell cultures from Drp1 cKO mice. Contrary to control mice (Figure 2), no difference in PA-induced maximal oxygen consumption rate was observed in high (2.5 mM) (Figure 3g,h) or low glucose (0.5 mM) (Figure 3i,j).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse XF96 Analyzer measurements, referenced in Figure 3.

claim: No effects induced by etomoxir incubation were observed in primary hypothalamic neurons derived from Drp1 cKO mice.
source: In addition, no effects induced by etomoxir incubation were observed in primary hypothalamic neurons derived from Drp1 cKO mice (Figure 3g–j), indicating that DRP1 in the hypothalamic AgRP neurons plays an essential role in regulating PA-induced mitochondrial respiration.
evidence: Supported by Seahorse XF96 Analyzer measurements, referenced in Figure 3.

claim: DRP1 in the hypothalamic AgRP neurons plays an essential role in regulating PA-induced mitochondrial respiration.
source: In addition, no effects induced by etomoxir incubation were observed in primary hypothalamic neurons derived from Drp1 cKO mice (Figure 3g–j), indicating that DRP1 in the hypothalamic AgRP neurons plays an essential role in regulating PA-induced mitochondrial respiration.
evidence: Inferred from the loss of palmitate-induced oxygen consumption response in Drp1 cKO neurons.

claim: Fasted Drp1 cKO male mice showed a significant decrease in immunoreactivity for Fos in AgRP neurons at bregma −1.70 mm (25.1 ± 3.83%) compared to fasted controls (37.0 ± 2.95%; p=0.0336).
source: Compared to fasted controls (bregma −1.70 mm: 37.0 ± 2.95% of AgRP neurons, n = 6, Figure 4a,c,e,g; bregma −1.46 mm: 40.6 ± 2.71% of AgRP neurons, n = 5, Figure 4g, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–c; bregma −2.06 mm: 36.4 ± 3.97% of AgRP neurons, n = 6; total 39.14 ± 2.925% of AgRP neurons, n = 6, Figure 4g, Figure 4—figure supplement 1g–i), fasted Drp1 cKO male mice showed a significant decrease in immunoreactivity for Fos in AgRP neurons (bregma −1.70 mm: 25.1 ± 3.83% of AgRP neurons, n = 5, p=0.0336, Figure 4b,d,f,g
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry quantification with statistical significance p=0.0336, referenced in Figure 4.

claim: Fasted Drp1 cKO male mice showed a significant decrease in immunoreactivity for Fos in AgRP neurons at bregma −1.46 mm (22.6 ± 4.15%) compared to fasted controls (40.6 ± 2.71%; p=0.0069).
source: bregma −1.46 mm: 22.6 ± 4.15% of AgRP neurons, n = 4, p=0.0069, Figure 4g, Figure 4—figure supplement 1d–f
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry quantification with statistical significance p=0.0069, referenced in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fasted Drp1 cKO male mice showed a significant decrease in immunoreactivity for Fos in AgRP neurons at bregma −2.06 mm (21.6 ± 4.82%) compared to fasted controls (36.4 ± 3.97%; p=0.0455).
source: bregma −2.06 mm: 21.6 ± 4.82% of AgRP neurons, n = 4, p=0.0455; total, 24.2 ± 3.58% of AgRP neurons, n = 6, p=0.0097, Figure 4g, Figure 4—figure supplement 1j–l)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry quantification with statistical significance p=0.0455, referenced in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: No changes in AgRP cell number were observed between control and Drp1 cKO male mice across different bregma coordinates.
source: No changes in AgRP cell number were observed between control (bregma −1.46 mm, 136.2 ± 10.71 counts, n = 5; bregma −1.70 mm, 142.3 ± 7.89 counts, n = 6; bregma −2.06 mm, 142.7 ± 8.841 counts, n = 6) and Drp1 cKO male mice (bregma −1.46 mm, 147.5 ± 1.50 counts, n = 4, p=0.3858; bregma −1.70 mm, 154.0 ± 3.48 counts, n = 5, p=0.2397; bregma −2.06 mm, 148.0 ± 3.89 counts, n = 4, p=0.6395; total, 150.833 ± 2.753 counts, n = 5, p=0.3467, Figure 4h).
evidence: Supported by cell counting showing no significant differences, referenced in Figure 4h.

claim: A significant reduction in overnight fasting-induced food intake was observed in Drp1 cKO mice (5.155 ± 0.294 g) compared to controls (6.391 ± 0.290 g; p=0.005).
source: In agreement with reduced AgRP neuronal activation, a significant reduction in overnight fasting-induced food intake was observed in Drp1 cKO mice (5.155 ± 0.294 g, n = 11, p=0.005) compared to controls (6.391 ± 0.290 g, n = 11, Figure 4i).
evidence: Supported by food intake measurements with statistical significance p=0.005, referenced in Figure 4i.

claim: A significant decrease in the PVN AgRP fluorescent intensity was observed in fasted Drp1 cKO male mice compared to controls at bregma −0.70 mm (Drp1 cKO = 0.4372 ± 0.0864 vs control = 1.000 ± 0.1175; p=0.0084).
source: We observed that compared to controls, a significant decrease in the PVN AgRP fluorescent intensity (bregma −0.70 mm: control = 1.000 ± 0.1175, n = 4; Drp1 cKO mice = 0.4372 ± 0.0864, n = 4, p=0.0084, Figure 5a–c
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification with statistical significance p=0.0084, referenced in Figure 5.

claim: A significant decrease in the PVN AgRP fluorescent intensity was observed in fasted Drp1 cKO male mice compared to controls at bregma −0.82 mm (Drp1 cKO = 0.3182 ± 0.032222 vs control = 1.000 ± 0.03906; p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification with statistical significance p<0.0001, referenced in Figure 5.

claim: A significant decrease in the PVN AgRP fluorescent intensity was observed in fasted Drp1 cKO male mice compared to controls at bregma −0.94 mm (Drp1 cKO = 0.6318 ± 0.06872 vs control = 1.000 ± 0.1158; p=0.0340).
source: bregma −0.94 mm: control = 1.000 ± 0.1158, n = 4; Drp1 cKO mice = 0.6318 ± 0.06872, n = 4, p=0.0340, Figure 5i–k
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification with statistical significance p=0.0340, referenced in Figure 5.

claim: A significant decrease in the PVN AgRP fluorescent intensity was observed in fasted Drp1 cKO male mice compared to controls at bregma −1.06 mm (Drp1 cKO = 0.5641 ± 0.04275 vs control = 1.000 ± 0.1267; p=0.0173).
source: bregma −1.06 mm: control = 1.000 ± 0.1267, n = 4; Drp1 cKO mice = 0.5641 ± 0.04275, n = 4, p=0.0173, Figure 5m–o)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification with statistical significance p=0.0173, referenced in Figure 5.

claim: A significant decrease in AgRP particle number in the PVN was observed in fasted Drp1 cKO male mice compared to controls at bregma −0.70 mm (Drp1 cKO = 673 ± 42.15 vs control = 885.25 ± 36.16; p=0.0087).
source: and particle number (bregma −0.70 mm: control = 885.25 ± 36.16 counts, n = 4; Drp1 cKO mice = 673 ± 42.15, n = 4, p=0.0087, Figure 5d
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification with statistical significance p=0.0087, referenced in Figure 5.

claim: A significant decrease in AgRP particle number in the PVN was observed in fasted Drp1 cKO male mice compared to controls at bregma −0.82 mm (Drp1 cKO = 777.6 ± 14.84 vs control = 899.5 ± 22.15; p=0.0038).
source: bregma −0.82 mm: control = 899.5 ± 22.15 counts, n = 4; Drp1 cKO mice = 777.6 ± 14.84, n = 4, p=0.0038, Figure 5h
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification with statistical significance p=0.0038, referenced in Figure 5.

claim: A significant decrease in AgRP particle number in the PVN was observed in fasted Drp1 cKO male mice compared to controls at bregma −0.94 mm (Drp1 cKO = 821.4 ± 24.35 vs control = 965.6 ± 25.88; p=0.0067).
source: bregma −0.94 mm: control = 965.6 ± 25.88 counts, n = 4; Drp1 cKO mice = 821.4 ± 24.35, n = 4, p=0.0067, Figure 5l
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification with statistical significance p=0.0067, referenced in Figure 5.

claim: A significant decrease in AgRP particle number in the PVN was observed in fasted Drp1 cKO male mice compared to controls at bregma −1.06 mm (Drp1 cKO = 848.5 ± 18.79 vs control = 979 ± 11.64; p=0.0010).
source: bregma −1.06 mm: control = 979 ± 11.64 counts, n = 4; Drp1 cKO mice = 848.5 ± 18.79, n = 4, p=0.0010, Figure 5p)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification with statistical significance p=0.0010, referenced in Figure 5.

claim: A significant increase in POMC cells immunoreactive for Fos was observed in Drp1 cKO mice (33.683 ± 2.050%) compared to controls (22.169 ± 1.297%; p=0.0032).
source: A significant increase in POMC cells immunoreactive for Fos was observed in Drp1 cKO mice (33.683 ± 2.050% of POMC neurons, n = 4, p=0.0032) compared to controls (22.169 ± 1.297% of POMC neurons, n = 4, Figure 5—figure supplement 1a–g).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry quantification with statistical significance p=0.0032, referenced in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: No changes in POMC cell number were observed between control and Drp1 cKO mice.
source: No changes in POMC cell number were observed between control and Drp1 cKO mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: Supported by cell counting, referenced in Figure 5—figure supplement 1h.

claim: Significant increases in relative intensity of α-MSH fibers were observed in the PVN of Drp1 cKO mice (6.195 ± 0.494) compared to controls (1.000 ± 0.164; p<0.0001).
source: Significant increases in relative intensity (control = 1.000 ± 0.164 counts, n = 4; Drp1 cKO mice = 6.195 ± 0.494, n = 5, p<0.0001, Figure 5—figure supplement 1k)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification with statistical significance p<0.0001, referenced in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Significant increases in particle number of α-MSH fibers were observed in the PVN of Drp1 cKO mice (393.400 ± 19.290) compared to controls (157.625 ± 13.488; p<0.0001).
source: and particle number (control = 157.625 ± 13.488 counts, n = 4; Drp1 cKO mice = 393.400 ± 19.290 counts, n = 5, p<0.0001, Figure 5—figure supplement 1l)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification with statistical significance p<0.0001, referenced in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A significant increase in Fos immunopositive cells in the PVN was observed in fasted Drp1 cKO mice (72.600 ± 9.092) compared to controls (22.750 ± 4.535; p=0.0028).
source: In agreement with a reduced AgRP and an increased POMC neuronal activation, we observed a significant increase in Fos immunopositive cells in the PVN of fasted Drp1 cKO mice (72.600 ± 9.092 counts, n = 5, p=0.0028) compared to their controls (22.750 ± 4.535 counts, n = 4, Figure 5—figure supplement 1m–o).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry quantification with statistical significance p=0.0028, referenced in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dnm1l mRNA transcript was significantly downregulated in AgRP neurons of fasted Drp1 cKO mice (1.361 ± 0.294) compared to fasted control mice (4.488 ± 0.685; p=0.00301).
source: Quantitative real time-PCR analyses revealed that Dnm1l mRNA transcript (fasted control = 4.488 ± 0.685, n = 5; fasted Drp1 cKO = 1.361 ± 0.294, n = 5; p=0.00301, Figure 5—figure supplement 2a) was significantly downregulated in AgRP neurons of fasted Drp1 cKO mice compared to fasted control mice, validating the arcuate AgRP neuronal isolation protocol and the mouse model for conditional deletion of Dnm1l in AgRP neurons.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data with statistical significance p=0.00301, referenced in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: No significant differences in Agrp and Pomc mRNA levels in the arcuate nucleus were observed between fasted controls and Drp1 cKO mice.
source: However, no significant differences in Agrp (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b) and Pomc mRNA levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 2c) in the arcuate nucleus were observed between fasted controls and Drp1 cKO mice.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing no significant differences, referenced in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: A significant decrease in body weight of Drp1 cKO male mice compared to controls was observed 3 weeks after the start of TMX treatment and was maintained through the end of the study when the mice were 20 weeks old.
source: A significant decrease in body weight of Drp1 cKO male mice compared to controls was observed 3 weeks after the start of TMX treatment (Figure 6a) and was maintained through the end of the study when the mice were 20 weeks old (Figure 6a; n = 17 per group).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal body weight measurements, referenced in Figure 6a.

claim: The decrease in body weight of Drp1 cKO male mice was associated with a significant reduction in fat mass (p<0.0001).
source: The decrease in body weight of Drp1 cKO male mice was associated with a significant reduction in fat mass (Figure 6b; n = 22, p<0.0001)
evidence: Supported by MRI body composition measurements with statistical significance p<0.0001, referenced in Figure 6b.

claim: No significant difference in lean mass was observed between Drp1 cKO male mice and controls (p=0.3421).
source: while no significant difference in lean mass was observed (Figure 6c; n = 22, p=0.3421) compared to control mice.
evidence: Supported by MRI body composition measurements showing no significant difference (p=0.3421), referenced in Figure 6c.

claim: Drp1 cKO mice showed significantly lower food intake compared to controls (Drp1 cKO = 3.366 ± 0.139 g vs control = 4.181 ± 0.124 g; p<0.0001).
source: Drp1 cKO mice showed significantly lower food intake compared to controls (control = 4.181 ± 0.124 g, n = 14; Drp1 cKO mice = 3.366 ± 0.139 g, n = 18, p<0.0001, total in Figure 6d,e)
evidence: Supported by food intake measurements with statistical significance p<0.0001, referenced in Figure 6.

claim: The lower food intake in Drp1 cKO mice was due to a significant reduction of food intake during the dark period (Drp1 cKO = 2.471 ± 0.120 g vs control = 2.937 ± 0.137 g; p=0.0236).
source: due to a significant reduction of food intake during the dark period (control = 2.937 ± 0.137 g, n = 14; Drp1 cKO mice = 2.471 ± 0.120 g, n = 18, p=0.0236, dark in Figure 6e).
evidence: Supported by food intake measurements during dark phase with statistical significance p=0.0236, referenced in Figure 6e.

claim: A significant increase in locomotor activity was observed in Drp1 cKO mice compared to controls (Drp1 cKO = 108400.917 ± 17432.685 vs control = 50122.750 ± 5919.799 beam-break counts; p=0.0008).
source: A significant increase in locomotor activity was observed in Drp1 cKO mice compared to controls (control = 50122.750 ± 5919.799 beam-break counts, n = 14; Drp1 cKO mice = 108400.917 ± 17432.685 beam-break counts, n = 18, p=0.0008, Figure 6f)
evidence: Supported by metabolic cage measurements with statistical significance p=0.0008, referenced in Figure 6f.

claim: The increase in locomotor activity in Drp1 cKO mice was due to a significant increase during the dark period (Drp1 cKO = 80081.806 ± 13085.949 vs control = 35556.429 ± 4272.846 counts; p=0.0136).
source: which was due to a significant increase during the dark period (control = 35556.429 ± 4272.846 counts, n = 14; Drp1 cKO mice = 80081.806 ± 13085.949 counts, n = 18, p=0.0136, Figure 6f).
evidence: Supported by metabolic cage measurements during dark phase with statistical significance p=0.0136, referenced in Figure 6f.

claim: Drp1 cKO mice showed significantly increased energy expenditure compared to controls (Drp1 cKO = 337.096 ± 7.218 vs control = 303.329 ± 5.760; p<0.0001).
source: The difference in body weight and composition were also associated with significantly increased energy expenditure (control = 303.329 ± 5.760, n = 14; Drp1 cKO mice = 337.096 ± 7.218, n = 18, p<0.0001, Figure 6g–i)
evidence: Supported by metabolic cage measurements with statistical significance p<0.0001, referenced in Figure 6.

claim: Drp1 cKO mice showed increased O2 consumption compared to controls (Drp1 cKO = 1345.19 ± 31.46 vs control = 1245.16 ± 29.94; p=0.0318).
source: increased O2 consumption (control = 1245.16 ± 29.94, n = 14; Drp1 cKO mice = 1345.19 ± 31.46, n = 18, p=0.0318, Figure 6j)
evidence: Supported by metabolic cage measurements with statistical significance p=0.0318, referenced in Figure 6j.

claim: Drp1 cKO mice showed increased CO2 production compared to controls (Drp1 cKO = 1248.44 ± 27.15 vs control = 1140.4 ± 28.18; p=0.0105).
source: and CO2 production (control = 1140.4 ± 28.18, n = 14; Drp1 cKO mice = 1248.44 ± 27.15, n = 18, p=0.0105, Figure 6k)
evidence: Supported by metabolic cage measurements with statistical significance p=0.0105, referenced in Figure 6k.

claim: No significant differences in the respiration exchange rate (RER) were observed between Drp1 cKO mice and control mice (Drp1 cKO = 0.8734 ± 0.00852 vs control = 0.8855 ± 0.007676; p=0.3133).

evidence: Supported by metabolic cage measurements showing no significant difference (p=0.3133), referenced in Figure 6l.

claim: BAT temperature was significantly increased in Drp1 cKO mice compared to control mice (Drp1 cKO = 35.038 ± 0.318°C vs control = 33.388 ± 0.223°C; p=0.0008).
source: We found that BAT temperature was significantly increased in Drp1 cKO mice compared to control mice (control = 33.388 ± 0.223°C, n = 8; Drp1 cKO mice = 35.038 ± 0.318°C, n = 8, p=0.0008, Figure 6—figure supplement 2a–c).
evidence: Supported by infrared thermography measurements with statistical significance p=0.0008, referenced in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Rectal temperature was significantly increased in Drp1 cKO mice compared to controls (Drp1 cKO = 37.300 ± 0.105°C vs control = 36.654 ± 0.226°C; p=0.0283).
source: Rectal temperature was also significantly increased in Drp1 cKO mice (37.300 ± 0.105°C, n = 8) compared to controls (36.654 ± 0.226°C, n = 8; p=0.0283, Figure 6—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: Supported by rectal temperature measurements with statistical significance p=0.0283, referenced in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The rectal temperature of female Drp1 cKO mice was significantly greater than that of female controls (Drp1 cKO = 37.181 ± 0.085°C vs control = 36.652 ± 0.142°C; p=0.0102).
source: Similar to males, the rectal temperature of female Drp1 cKO mice (37.181 ± 0.085°C, n = 7) was significantly greater than that of female controls (36.652 ± 0.142°C, n = 9; p=0.0102; Figure 6—figure supplement 2e).
evidence: Supported by rectal temperature measurements with statistical significance p=0.0102, referenced in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ghrelin, a gut-derived hormone secreted during food deprivation, promotes feeding behavior through NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: Ghrelin, a gut-derived hormone secreted during food deprivation, promotes feeding behavior through NPY/AgRP neurons (Andrews et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Andrews et al., 2008.

claim: A significant decrease in Fos immunoreactivity in AgRP neurons was found in ghrelin-treated Drp1 cKO mice (30.22 ± 4.652%) compared to controls (75.35 ± 3.464%; p=0.0001).
source: We found a significant decrease in Fos immunoreactivity in AgRP neurons of ghrelin-treated Drp1 cKO mice (30.22 ± 4.652% of AgRP neurons, n = 5, p=0.0001) compared to controls (75.35 ± 3.464% of AgRP neurons, n = 4, Figure 7a–g).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry quantification with statistical significance p=0.0001, referenced in Figure 7.

claim: No difference in the number of AgRP neurons in the ARC was observed between ghrelin-treated control and Drp1 cKO mice.
source: No difference in the number of AgRP neurons in the ARC was observed between the two groups (Figure 7h).
evidence: Supported by cell counting, referenced in Figure 7h.

claim: Ghrelin-induced hyperphagia was not observed in Drp1 cKO mice compared to controls.
source: In agreement with that, ghrelin-induced hyperphagia was not observed in Drp1 cKO mice compared to controls (Figure 7i).
evidence: Supported by food intake measurements after ghrelin injection, referenced in Figure 7i.

claim: Ghrelin significantly increased membrane potential in AgRP neurons of control mice (ghrelin = −43.757 ± 0.678 mV vs resting = −46.644 ± 0.502 mV; p=0.0102).
source: Consistent with the Fos results, ghrelin significantly increased membrane potential (resting = −46.644 ± 0.502 mV, n = 20; ghrelin = −43.757 ± 0.678 mV, n = 20, p=0.0102; Figure 7j,l)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology measurements with statistical significance p=0.0102, referenced in Figure 7.

claim: Ghrelin significantly increased relative firing activity of AgRP neurons in control mice (ghrelin = 186.894 ± 20.266 vs resting = 100.000 ± 14.584; p=0.0041).
source: and relative firing activity (resting = 100.000 ± 14.584, n = 22; ghrelin = 186.894 ± 20.266, n = 22, p=0.0041; Figure 7k,l)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology measurements with statistical significance p=0.0041, referenced in Figure 7.

claim: Ghrelin-induced excitation of AgRP neurons was significantly attenuated in Drp1 cKO mice compared to controls in terms of membrane potential (ghrelin = −45.677 ± 0.644 mV vs resting = −46.104 ± 0.577 mV; p=0.9962).
source: while ghrelin-induced excitation of AgRP neurons was significantly attenuated in Drp1 cKO mice compared to controls (membrane potential, resting = −46.104 ± 0.577 mV, n = 19; ghrelin = −45.677 ± 0.644 mV, n = 19, p=0.9962, Figure 7j,l
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology measurements showing no significant change (p=0.9962), referenced in Figure 7.

claim: Ghrelin-induced excitation of AgRP neurons was significantly attenuated in Drp1 cKO mice compared to controls in terms of relative firing activity (ghrelin = 119.985 ± 16.502 vs resting = 100.000 ± 15.106; p=0.9644).
source: relative firing activity, resting = 100.000 ± 15.106, n = 20; ghrelin = 119.985 ± 16.502, n = 20, p=0.9644, Figure 7k,l).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology measurements showing no significant change (p=0.9644), referenced in Figure 7.

claim: No differences in the total and active form of ghrelin levels were observed between male control and Drp1 cKO mice in either fed or fasted states.
source: Of note, no differences in the total (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a) and active form of ghrelin levels (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b) were observed between male control and Drp1 cKO mice in either fed or fasted states.
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements, referenced in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission plays a critical role in regulating ghrelin-triggered AgRP neuronal activity and hyperphagia.
source: Together, these data suggest that DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission plays a critical role in regulating ghrelin-triggered AgRP neuronal activity and hyperphagia.
evidence: Inferred from the attenuated ghrelin responses in Drp1 cKO mice.

claim: DRP1-driven mitochondrial fission in AgRP neurons is an adaptive process enabling these neurons to respond to the changing metabolic environment.
source: Altogether, these data revealed that DRP1-driven mitochondrial fission in AgRP neurons is an adaptive process enabling these neurons to respond to the changing metabolic environment.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of metabolic and neuronal phenotypes in Drp1 cKO mice.

claim: Mitochondrial dynamics through fusion and fission processes are important in maintaining mitochondrial quality control in order to maintain optimal mitochondrial bioenergetic functions.
source: Mitochondrial dynamics through fusion and fission processes are also important in maintaining mitochondrial quality control in order to maintain optimal mitochondrial bioenergetic functions (Twig et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Twig et al., 2008.

claim: Mitochondrial dynamics and specifically mitochondrial fission play an important role in sensing changes of nutrients availability in AgRP neurons.
source: Our data indicate that mitochondrial dynamics and specifically mitochondrial fission play an important role in sensing changes of nutrients availability in AgRP neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of mitochondrial morphology, respiration, and neuronal activity changes.

claim: In mice with AgRP-selective deletion of Mfn1 and Mfn2, neuronal firing frequency was impaired in diet-induced obesity mice.
source: In line with our results, Dietrich et al., 2013 have shown that in mice with AgRP-selective deletion of Mfn1 and Mfn2, mediators of mitochondrial fusion process, neuronal firing frequency was impaired in diet-induced obesity mice.
evidence: Supported by citation to Dietrich et al., 2013.

claim: The impairment of AgRP neuronal activation in Mfn1/Mfn2 deletion mice was reversed by increasing intracellular ATP levels.
source: The impairment of AgRP neuronal activation was reversed by increasing intracellular ATP levels (Dietrich et al., 2013), indicating that the impaired AgRP neuronal firing frequency is likely due to low intracellular ATP levels.
evidence: Supported by citation to Dietrich et al., 2013.

claim: DRP1 has been shown to enable peroxisomal fission.
source: In addition to mitochondria, DRP1 has been also shown to enable peroxisomal fission.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about DRP1 function.

claim: Peroxisomes are single-membrane organelles that catalyze the breakdown of long chain fatty acids through beta-oxidation and regulate the maintenance of redox homeostasis.
source: Peroxisomes are single-membrane organelles that similar to mitochondria catalyze the breakdown of long chain fatty acids through beta-oxidation and regulate the maintenance of redox homeostasis (Smith and Aitchison, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith and Aitchison, 2013.

claim: Mitochondrial fission in hypothalamic AgRP neurons is a fundamental mechanism that allows these neurons to sense and respond to changes in circulating signals, including hormones such as ghrelin and nutrients such as glucose and palmitic acid, in the regulation of feeding and energy metabolism.
source: Overall, our data unmask that mitochondrial fission in hypothalamic AgRP neurons is a fundamental mechanism that allows these neurons to sense and respond to changes in circulating signals, including hormones such as ghrelin and nutrients such as glucose and palmitic acid, in the regulation of feeding and energy metabolism.
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive set of observations in the study.

claim: The hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (ARC) contains two distinct neuronal subpopulations that produce either orexigenic neuropeptides agouti-related peptide (AgRP) and neuropeptide-Y (NPY), or anorexigenic neuropeptides including alpha-melanocyte stimulating hormone (α-MSH) derived from proopiomelanocortin (POMC).
source: The hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (ARC) contains two distinct neuronal subpopulations that produce either orexigenic neuropeptides agouti-related peptide (AgRP) and neuropeptide-Y (NPY), or anorexigenic neuropeptides including alpha-melanocyte stimulating hormone (α-MSH) derived from proopiomelanocortin (POMC) (Batterham et al., 2002; Ollmann et al., 1997; Roh et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Batterham et al., 2002; Ollmann et al., 1997; Roh et al., 2016.

claim: The anatomical location of the hypothalamic ARC allows these neurons to rapidly respond to fluctuations of numerous circulating metabolic signals, including nutrients and hormones.
source: The anatomical location of the hypothalamic ARC allows these neurons to rapidly respond to fluctuations of numerous circulating metabolic signals, including nutrients and hormones (Gao and Horvath, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gao and Horvath, 2007.

claim: Mitochondria are the main powerhouse of the cell by producing adenosine triphosphate (ATP).
source: Mitochondria are the main powerhouse of the cell by producing adenosine triphosphate (ATP) (Mattson et al., 2008; Picard et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mattson et al., 2008; Picard et al., 2016.

claim: Neurons rely on mitochondrial electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation to meet their high energy demands.
source: Neurons rely on mitochondrial electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation to meet their high energy demands (Bélanger et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bélanger et al., 2011.

claim: Mitochondria are highly dynamic organelles able to change their morphology and location according to the needs of the cell.
source: In addition, mitochondria are highly dynamic organelles able to change their morphology and location according to the needs of the cell (Chan, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chan, 2006.

claim: Mitochondrial morphological changes are associated with several proteins, including mitofusin 1 and 2 (MFN1 and MFN2) in the mitochondrial outer membrane and optic atrophy-1 (OPA1) in the mitochondrial inner membrane for mitochondrial fusion.
source: Mitochondrial morphological changes are associated with several proteins, including mitofusin 1 and 2 (MFN1 and MFN2) in the mitochondrial outer membrane and optic atrophy-1 (OPA1) in the mitochondrial inner membrane for mitochondrial fusion (Kasahara and Scorrano, 2014; Youle and van der Bliek, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kasahara and Scorrano, 2014; Youle and van der Bliek, 2012.

claim: Mitochondrial fission is regulated by the activity of the dynamin-related protein 1 (DRP1, a mechanochemical protein encoded by the Dnm1l gene), which is recruited to the mitochondrial outer membrane to interact with mitochondrial fission factor (Mff) and mitochondrial fission 1 (Fis1).
source: whereas mitochondrial fission is regulated by the activity of the dynamin-related protein 1 (DRP1, a mechanochemical protein encoded by the Dnm1l gene), which is recruited to the mitochondrial outer membrane to interact with mitochondrial fission factor (Mff) and mitochondrial fission 1 (Fis1) (Losón et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Losón et al., 2013.

claim: Previous studies have shown that NPY/AgRP neuronal activation is associated with changes in mitochondrial morphology and density during fasting or after ghrelin administration.
source: Previous studies from our laboratory have shown that NPY/AgRP neuronal activation is associated with changes in mitochondrial morphology and density during fasting or after ghrelin administration (Andrews et al., 2008; Coppola et al., 2007; Dietrich et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Andrews et al., 2008; Coppola et al., 2007; Dietrich et al., 2013.

claim: High-fat-diet-induced inactivation of NPY/AgRP neurons is associated with mitochondrial dynamics leaning towards mitochondrial fusion in this neuronal population.
source: In addition, we found that high-fat-diet-induced inactivation of NPY/AgRP neurons is associated with mitochondrial dynamics leaning towards mitochondrial fusion in this neuronal population (Dietrich et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dietrich et al., 2013.
